h1: Supply chain and procurement jobs in drinks companies
title: Supply Chain Jobs in Drinks Companies | Craft Beer School
desc: The supply chain and procurement roles in breweries, distilleries and wineries, what each one does and the drinks knowledge that helps.
teaser: Beer, whisky and wine all depend on farm crops, glass, cans and trucks arriving on time. Someone has to plan all of it.
standfirst: Drinks companies run long supply chains, from barley fields and vineyards to bars and shops across India. This guide explains the supply chain and procurement jobs inside them and what makes the drinks business different.
sections: Why drinks supply chains are unusual

A drinks supply chain starts on a farm. Barley, maize, rice, grapes and molasses all depend on harvests and weather. Hops for craft beer are mostly imported. Then come packaging materials such as glass, cans, crowns, labels and cartons, each with its own supplier and lead time.

At the other end, alcohol in India is heavily regulated. Every state sets its own rules for how drinks are taxed, moved and sold, so the route from brewery to shelf can differ from state to state. Our guide to the beer supply chain walks through the whole route.

Procurement teams buy everything the company needs to make and sell its drinks.

  • Raw material buyer: malt, grains, hops, sugar, grapes or grain spirit, depending on the company.
  • Packaging buyer: bottles, cans, closures, labels and cartons.
  • Indirect procurement: cleaning chemicals, spare parts, services and equipment.
  • Category manager: owns a group of materials and the long-term supplier strategy.

Buyers need to understand quality as well as price. A cheaper malt with poor extract or a bottle with a weak neck can cost far more in losses than it saves. Our guide to barley and malt for procurement teams explains what the specification numbers mean.

• Demand planner: forecasts how much of each product will sell, by pack and region.
  • Supply or production planner: turns the forecast into a brewing, distilling or bottling plan.
  • Materials planner: makes sure raw materials and packaging arrive in time for that plan.

In beer, demand in India peaks in the hot months and falls in the monsoon, so planners build stock ahead of summer. Beer also has a limited shelf life, so building too much stock is costly. Whisky planning works on a much longer clock because spirit must mature for years before it can be sold. Wine depends on one harvest a year. Our guide to beer production planning covers the beer side.

Logistics teams move finished goods from the plant to depots, distributors and retailers. In India this includes managing permits for moving alcohol between states and within them, which vary by state and change.

Returnable glass is common in mainstream Indian beer, which adds a reverse flow: empty bottles have to be collected, sorted, inspected and washed before reuse. Managing that loop well saves the company money. Temperature also matters. Beer and wine suffer in heat, so warehouses and transport in summer need attention.

Supply chain roles in drinks need the same core skills as in any manufacturing business: planning, negotiation, data analysis, supplier management and knowledge of systems such as ERP software.

What helps you stand out is understanding the product. A planner who knows why a lager needs several weeks in tank before it can be packaged makes better plans. A buyer who knows how hop freshness affects aroma asks better questions about storage. You do not need to brew, but knowing the process makes conversations with production easier.

Here is a small example. A malt delivery arrives with moisture above the agreed specification. A buyer who knows that wetter malt carries less extract per kilo and may not store well through the monsoon, can raise it with the supplier the same day instead of finding out weeks later from a yield report.
Getting into drinks supply chain work

People usually move in from FMCG, food manufacturing, logistics or retail supply chains, where the work is similar. Large drinks companies and their capability centres in cities such as Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune hire planners, analysts and buyers. Smaller breweries and distilleries often combine purchasing, planning and stock control in one role.

If you are early in your career, a supply chain or operations degree helps, as does experience with spreadsheets and planning systems. If you are moving from another industry, learn the drinks basics and talk about how your experience applies.

Supply chain people often progress to planning or procurement managers, then into operations or supply chain leadership. In smaller drinks businesses, someone who understands purchasing, planning and the product can become the operations lead the owner relies on. Learning how costs, stock and cash flow fit together is what makes that step possible.
faqs: Do I need a brewing background for supply chain jobs in drinks?
No. Most supply chain staff come from other industries. Learning the basics of how drinks are made helps you work well with production teams.
What makes drinks supply chains different?
Farm-based raw materials, seasonal demand, limited shelf life for beer, long maturation for whisky and state-by-state regulation in India.
Which industries move most easily into drinks supply chain roles?
FMCG, food manufacturing, logistics and retail, because the planning, buying and distribution work is similar.
